LEGAL PRINCIPLES ESTABLISHED (RATIO DECIDENDI):
For the purposes of Section 69 of the Evidence Act, when no attesting witness can be found, it is not sufficient to examine a stray witness who merely states he saw an attesting witness sign; the witness must be familiar with the handwriting/signature of the attesting witness. Statutory presumption of adoption under Section 16 HAMA does not dispense with the mandatory legal proof of a Will under which property rights are claimed.

- Substantive relevance: Substantively examines adoption claims under Section 16 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 in relation to testamentary succession and title to properties.

Following matrimonial discord, the appellant-wife registered an FIR in Rajasthan against her husband and in-laws for offences under Sections 498A, 406, and 323 IPC. Extra-territorial anticipatory bail or transit interim protection can be granted under Section 438 CrPC to prevent imminent threat of wrongful arrest violating Article 21, but it must be exercised sparingly and with caution so as not to undermine the territorial jurisdiction of the State where the offence was committed.

FACTS SUMMARY & MATRIMONIAL DISPUTE BACKGROUND:
Deceased Jayant Shivram Salgaonkar executed a Will in 2011 bequeathing his extensive estate among his legal heirs, but had previously nominated the appellants for certain mutual funds and company shares under Section 109A of the Companies Act, 1956. The nominees claimed absolute beneficial ownership over the shares to the exclusion of the legal heirs named in the Will.

Acts and Sections Invoked: Companies Act, 1956 [Sections: 109A, 109B]; Depositories Act, 1996; Hindu Succession Act, 1956 [Sections: 8, 10]; Indian Succession Act, 1925 [Sections: 211]

LEGAL PRINCIPLES ESTABLISHED (RATIO DECIDENDI):
Nomination under Section 109A of the Companies Act does not supersede the general laws of succession under the Hindu Succession Act or a testamentary Will. The nominee is merely authorized to receive the shares to discharge the company from liability, but the beneficial rights devolve exclusively onto legal heirs or legatees under succession law.

STATUTORY & JUDICIAL APPLICATION:
- Substantive relevance: Directly adjudicates the interrelation between statutory corporate nomination and the succession rights of legal heirs under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
- Decided by: HRISHIKESH ROY AND PANKAJ MITHAL

FACTS SUMMARY & MATRIMONIAL DISPUTE BACKGROUND:
Husband filed a petition for divorce under Section 13(1)(i) of the Hindu Marriage Act alleging adultery against his wife, and filed an interim application before the Family Court seeking a direction for their second minor child to undergo a DNA paternity test to establish the wife's alleged infidelity. The Family Court allowed the application, and the High Court affirmed the order.

case_name: APARNA AJINKYA FIRODIA v. AJINKYA ARUN FIRODIA
bench: V. RAMASUBRAMANIAN AND B.V. NAGARATHNA
content:
[PRECEDENT RATIO DECIDENDI & LEGAL PRINCIPLES]
Case: APARNA AJINKYA FIRODIA v. AJINKYA ARUN FIRODIA (2023)
Citation: [2023] 4 S.C.R. 680 | 2023 INSC 146
Sub-Case Type: Divorce / Paternity & DNA Testing
Acts and Sections Invoked: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 [Sections: 13(1)(i)]; Indian Evidence Act, 1872 [Sections: 112, 114]; Family Courts Act, 1984; Constitution of India [Sections: 21]

LEGAL PRINCIPLES ESTABLISHED (RATIO DECIDENDI):
Section 112 of the Evidence Act establishes a conclusive presumption of legitimacy that can only be displaced by strong and cogent proof of non-access during conception. DNA testing touches upon the child's constitutional right to privacy, dignity, and legitimacy and cannot be ordered as a matter of course or as a shortcut to prove adultery. Refusal to submit a child to DNA testing does not invite adverse inference under Section 114(h) where access is admitted.

STATUTORY & JUDICIAL APPLICATION:
- Substantive relevance: Core matrimonial proceeding under Section 13(1)(i) HMA and Family Courts Act laying down governing principles for ordering DNA paternity tests in divorce proceedings.
- Decided by: V. RAMASUBRAMANIAN AND B.V. NAGARATHNA

DNA testing touches upon the child's constitutional right to privacy, dignity, and legitimacy and cannot be ordered as a matter of course or as a shortcut to prove adultery. Refusal to submit a child to DNA testing does not invite adverse inference under Section 114(h) where access is admitted.

- Whether the grounds of reasonable restriction on free speech under Article 19(2) are exhaustive.
- Whether fundamental rights under Articles 19 and 21 can be enforced horizontally against private non-state actors.
- Whether statements made by Ministers can be vicariously attributed to the State.

HOLDING:
Reference answered. Restrictions under Article 19(2) are exhaustive and cannot be expanded by judicial interpretation; fundamental rights under Articles 19 and 21 can be enforced against persons other than the State; a Minister's statement cannot be vicariously attributed to the State unless it represents official government policy.

RATIO DECIDENDI:
Articles 19 and 21 have horizontal application against private parties and non-state entities. No extra restrictions beyond Article 19(2) can be imposed on the freedom of speech of public functionaries.

LEGAL PRINCIPLES ESTABLISHED (RATIO DECIDENDI):
Under Section 12 HAMA, an adopted child is deemed to be the child of the adoptive parents only from the date of adoption; the old shastric doctrine of relation back does not apply post-1956. For service pension purposes under CCS Rules, 'child' means a child born or adopted during the lifetime of the employee or during the subsistence of the marriage before death.

LEGAL PRINCIPLES ESTABLISHED (RATIO DECIDENDI):
Section 16(3) HMA restricts children's rights to the property of their parents, barring direct coparcenary rights in the larger joint family. However, under Section 6 HSA, upon the death of a coparcener, the parent's share is ascertained through a notional partition, and that share devolves upon all Class-I legal heirs, including children recognized as legitimate under Section 16 HMA.

STATUTORY & JUDICIAL APPLICATION:
- Substantive relevance: Landmark 3-Judge Bench judgment directly interpreting the property and coparcenary inheritance rights of children of void and voidable marriages under Section 16 HMA and Section 6 HSA.
- Decided by: Supreme Court Bench

Common ancestor 'P' died in 1959 leaving behind sons, daughters, and a widow. A partition suit was filed regarding agricultural coparcenary properties. Acts and Sections Invoked: Hindu Succession Act, 1956 [Sections: 6, 8]; Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 [Sections: 100]

LEGAL PRINCIPLES ESTABLISHED (RATIO DECIDENDI):
Under unamended Section 6 of HSA 1956, when a male Hindu died possessing an undivided coparcenary interest leaving female Class-I relatives, his interest devolved by intestate succession under Section 8 rather than survivorship. To determine the share, a notional partition is deemed immediately before his death, allocating shares to the coparceners and widow, and the deceased's share is then distributed equally among all Class-I heirs.

STATUTORY & JUDICIAL APPLICATION:
- Substantive relevance: Directly interprets devolution of coparcenary interest and notional partition under Section 6 and Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
- Decided by: C. T. RAVIKUMAR AND SANJAY KUMAR

LEGAL PRINCIPLES ESTABLISHED (RATIO DECIDENDI):
Section 7-A HMA authorizes Self-Respect marriages without traditional religious ceremonies, requiring only that the parties declare each other husband and wife in the presence of relatives, friends, or other persons. Advocates acting in their personal capacity or as friends are not disqualified from witnessing or certifying such marriages.

LEGAL PRINCIPLES ESTABLISHED (RATIO DECIDENDI):
Matrimonial cruelty must be assessed on a preponderance of probabilities rather than proof beyond reasonable doubt. When parties have lived apart for over a decade with severe mutual accusations destroying the emotional substratum, forcing them to remain tied in marriage constitutes mental cruelty under Section 13(1)(ia) HMA.

STATUTORY & JUDICIAL APPLICATION:
- Substantive relevance: Core matrimonial case under Section 13(1)(ia) HMA clarifying standard of proof for mental cruelty and granting decree of divorce.

Acts and Sections: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 [Sections: 13(1)(ia), 13(1)(ib)]; Constitution of India [Sections: 142]

FACTS:
The parties married in 2002 and separated in 2007. The wife filed for divorce on grounds of cruelty under Section 13(1)(ia) HMA. Both spouses leveled serious character allegations and criminal cases against each other and lived separately for over 15 years. Trial Court and High Court dismissed the divorce petition citing lack of independent corroboration.

ISSUES:
- Whether the lower courts adopted an erroneous hyper-technical standard of proof in declining divorce on grounds of mental cruelty under Section 13(1)(ia) HMA.
- Whether protracted separation and unsubstantiated character allegations constitute mental cruelty.

HOLDING:
Appeal allowed. Judgments of trial court and High Court set aside; decree of divorce granted dissolving the marriage.

RATIO DECIDENDI:
Matrimonial cruelty must be assessed on a preponderance of probabilities rather than proof beyond reasonable doubt. When parties have lived apart for over a decade with severe mutual accusations destroying the emotional substratum, forcing them to remain tied in marriage constitutes mental cruelty under Section 13(1)(ia) HMA.

LEGAL PRINCIPLES ESTABLISHED (RATIO DECIDENDI):
Under Section 15(1)(a) read with Section 16 (Rule 1) of HSA 1956, the heirs of a female Hindu dying intestate include the sons, daughters, and children of any pre-deceased son or daughter. By virtue of the branch representation rule, the widow of a pre-deceased son steps into her husband's shoes to inherit the share that would have fallen to the pre-deceased son.

STATUTORY & JUDICIAL APPLICATION:
- Substantive relevance: Directly interprets Section 15(1)(a) and Section 16 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 regarding inheritance rights of the widow of a pre-deceased son.

Under Section 36 of the Divorce Act, 1869, interim maintenance must ensure that the wife can sustain a standard of living reasonably comparable to the matrimonial lifestyle. Reduction of maintenance without factual justification is impermissible.

LEGAL PRINCIPLES ESTABLISHED (RATIO DECIDENDI):

Appellant-daughter filed a partition suit under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 claiming coparcenary share in ancestral family properties. Single Judge of High Court dismissed the partition suit on admissions under Order XII Rule 6 CPC on its own motion without formal application.

ISSUES:
- Whether a partition suit claiming coparcenary rights under Section 6 HSA can be dismissed suo motu under Order XII Rule 6 CPC without full trial on disputed questions of joint family nucleus and partition.

HOLDING:
Appeal dismissed on merits upholding the finding that properties had ceased to be coparcenary assets.

RATIO DECIDENDI:
Judgment on admissions under Order XII Rule 6 CPC can be exercised where clear and unambiguous admissions demonstrate that properties are not joint family assets capable of partition under Section 6 HSA.
